items.headline: A new piano drama is airing this week
items.body: "Four Hands, Two Sonatas" runs on tvN with Song Kang and Lee Jun Young as two arts-school students who become friends and rivals. If you are building a watch list, this is the one starting now.

items.headline: You still do not need a K-ETA — but you do need the arrival card
items.body: Travellers from 22 countries, including the US, UK, Canada, Australia and Japan, stay exempt from K-ETA until 31 December 2026. Most visitors now submit a digital e-Arrival Card before flying instead.

items.headline: Water is free, and you usually pour it yourself
items.body: In most Korean restaurants water and the small side dishes come free, and refills are free too. Look for the water jug and cups stacked near the door or on a shelf — staff will not bring them to you.

items.headline: Autumn leaves will come late this year — Seoraksan turns on 3 October
items.body: The Korea Tourism Organization’s 2026 forecast puts the first colour on Seoraksan on 3 October, with the peak around 25 October, and Bukhansan above Seoul peaking about 4 November. If you are planning a mountain trip, mid-October to early November is the window — the dates move with the weather.

items.headline: Since 2023 Korea counts age the way everyone else does
items.body: Until June 2023 many Koreans gave their “Korean age”, which could run a year or two higher than their international age. Documents and the law now use only international age (만 나이), though you will still hear the old way in casual talk — so “how old are you?” can get two answers.

items.headline: Chuseok is next week — book trains and hotels now
items.body: Chuseok, the harvest holiday, falls on Friday 25 September; the official holiday runs Thursday 24 to Saturday 26, so most people are off through Sunday. Offices and many small restaurants close, while the subway, convenience stores, malls and big sights stay open. KTX seats and central hotels sell out first.

items.headline: Songpyeon: the half-moon rice cake families make for Chuseok
items.body: Songpyeon are small rice cakes filled with sesame, chestnut or sweet beans and steamed on a bed of pine needles, which is where the name comes from. Families traditionally shape them together the night before Chuseok, and every market and department store is full of them this week.

items.headline: Read outdoors in the middle of Seoul — free, Fridays to Sundays
items.body: The Seoul Outdoor Library puts out beanbags and thousands of books on Seoul Plaza, Gwanghwamun Square and along Cheonggyecheon every Friday to Sunday until 1 November. No ticket and no library card — sit down and stay as long as you like.

items.headline: One card for every bus, subway and taxi
items.body: A T-money card from any convenience store works on public transport nationwide and gives you the transfer discount, so a bus-to-subway trip costs less than two separate fares. Top it up in cash at the store or at the machines in subway stations.

items.headline: “The Scandal” lands on Netflix today
items.body: Son Ye Jin and Ji Chang Wook lead this Joseon-era romance, a period retelling of Dangerous Liaisons with Nana in the cast. It is a full historical drama — palaces, hanbok and the formal speech you hear in sageuk.

items.headline: What Chuseok actually is
items.body: Chuseok is the harvest festival on the fifteenth day of the eighth lunar month. Families gather, set a table of food for their ancestors and visit the family graves — the closest thing Korea has to Thanksgiving, and the one week a year when Seoul empties out.

items.headline: A free orchestra concert in the park tonight
items.body: The Seoul Philharmonic plays outdoors at Seoul Children’s Grand Park from 7 pm to 8:20 pm — no ticket, no reservation. Bring a mat and arrive as the sun goes down.

items.headline: Guro’s Asian culture festival runs this weekend along Anyangcheon
items.body: The Guro G Festival fills the stream banks between Gocheokgyo and Ogeumgyo bridges with food, stalls and performances from across Asia on 19 and 20 September. Take Line 1 to Guro or Line 2 to Guro Digital Complex.

items.headline: The Seoul Autumn Festival starts tomorrow and runs to 29 November
items.body: Two months of open-air events across the city, from riverside shows on the Hangang to the fireworks festival in October. The city government’s English site posts each week’s line-up.

items.headline: The one Chuseok greeting you can say to anyone
items.body: “추석 잘 보내세요” — have a good Chuseok — works for a shopkeeper, a colleague or a host family. Drop the ending for friends: “추석 잘 보내”. Say it any time this week; nobody waits for the day itself.

items.headline: Andong’s mask dance festival opens Thursday and runs through Chuseok
items.body: The Andong International Mask Dance Festival runs 24 September to 4 October at Talchum Park and around Andong station, with the Hahoe village mask dance at its centre. Andong is about two and a half hours from Seoul by train, which makes it a natural holiday trip.

items.headline: Busan’s film festival is 6–15 October
items.body: The 31st Busan International Film Festival runs for ten days around the Busan Cinema Center, with more than three hundred films and dozens of world premieres. Popular screenings sell out within minutes of tickets opening, so watch the official site.

items.headline: Forty years of a textile pioneer go on show today at the craft museum
items.body: The Seoul Museum of Craft Art opens “Equinox: Autumn and Spring” on Tuesday 22 September, a retrospective of Chang Eung-bok, one of Korea’s first-generation textile designers. It is free, on the third floor of Exhibition Building 1, and stays up until 7 March 2027 — Tuesday to Sunday, 10 am to 6 pm, closed Mondays.

items.headline: Roads out of Seoul jam from Wednesday afternoon — here is when to move
items.body: Half the country heads to its 고향, the family hometown, this week. TMAP’s forecast puts the worst traffic out of Seoul on Wednesday afternoon and Thursday — a drive to Daejeon that normally takes under three hours is expected to take over four at 3 pm on Wednesday — and the heaviest traffic back into Seoul on Chuseok Day itself, Friday 25 September, from 8 am. If you are driving, Saturday and Sunday are the quieter days.

items.headline: Every royal palace in Seoul is free from Thursday to Sunday
items.body: Gyeongbokgung, Changdeokgung, Deoksugung and Changgyeonggung, plus Jongmyo Shrine and the Joseon royal tombs, waive admission from 24 to 27 September with no closing day. Jongmyo, normally a timed guided tour only, can be wandered freely, and the guard-changing ceremony at Gyeongbokgung runs at 10 am and 2 pm with no booking. Changdeokgung’s Secret Garden is the one exception and still needs its own ticket.

items.headline: Why every supermarket is stacked with boxes of Spam this week
items.body: Koreans give gift sets to relatives, friends and business contacts before Chuseok, and companies hand them to staff. Fruit, health supplements and beef top the surveys, but the flat boxes of canned ham, tuna and cooking oil are the ones that surprise visitors — canned ham has been a holiday gift since the 1980s, and about 60 percent of Spam sales come from the two big holidays. Stores clear whole aisles for them one to two weeks ahead.

items.headline: Namsangol Hanok Village throws a three-day Chuseok festival from Friday
items.body: Namsan Dalbit Madang runs Friday to Sunday, 25–27 September, 10 am to 8 pm, in the old houses of Namsangol Hanok Village near Chungmuro station. Expect traditional performances, hanbok to try on, old-fashioned games and a Korean food market. Entry is free; some activities and food are charged.

items.headline: Museums are free this holiday — but most close on Chuseok Day itself
items.body: The National Museum of Korea opens on 24, 26 and 27 September with free traditional music and dance performances each day, and all four MMCA branches are free for the whole four-day break. The National Museum, the National Folk Museum and MMCA Seoul close on Friday 25 September, so make Thursday or the weekend your museum day. The Folk Museum’s “All Together for Hangawi” adds ssireum wrestling and jegichagi, a game a bit like hacky sack.

items.headline: Tonight’s Chuseok moon rises over Seoul at 5:34 pm
items.body: Chuseok falls on the full moon of the eighth lunar month, and going out to look at it is part of the day. In Seoul the moon comes up at about 5:34 pm on Friday and 5:59 pm on Saturday — but it is only perfectly full at 1:49 am on Sunday, so Saturday night is the rounder one if you want a photo.

items.headline: Jeon: the pan-fried slices that fill every Chuseok kitchen
items.body: Jeon are slices of meat, vegetables or seafood coated in flour and egg and fried in a shallow pan, and the smell of them frying is the smell of the holiday. Families make stacks for the ancestral table and eat the rest for days. They are on restaurant menus year-round too — look for 모둠전, an assorted plate.

items.headline: Try tuho and jegichagi at two Seoul museums today
items.body: The Seoul Baekje Museum in Olympic Park holds its Chuseok festival on Saturday 26 September from 10 am to 5 pm, with performances, hands-on crafts and traditional games. Across town the Seoul Urban Life Museum runs gugak music, a magic show, tuho arrow-tossing, jegichagi and pouch-making from 1 to 5 pm. Both are free.

items.headline: Hangawi: the other name for Chuseok
items.body: You will see 한가위 on banners and hear it in greetings this week. It is the older, native-Korean name for the holiday, literally “the great middle” of autumn — the full moon in the middle of the eighth lunar month. 추석 is the Sino-Korean name; both mean the same day, and “즐거운 한가위 보내세요” works just as well as the Chuseok version.

items.headline: “Four Hands, Two Sonatas” plays its last episode next Sunday
items.body: Song Kang’s piano drama reaches its finale on Netflix on Sunday 4 October, with new episodes still landing on Saturdays and Sundays until then — this is the week to catch up. The next weekly K-dramas follow straight after: the medical remake “Doctor X” from 9 October and the colonial-era spy drama “100 Days of Deception” from 10 October.

items.headline: 1330: the number to call when you are stuck
items.body: The Korea Travel Helpline answers on 1330 — from abroad +82-2-1330 — for anything from a lost bag to which bus to take, and it also has a text chat in Korean, English, Japanese, Chinese, Russian, Vietnamese, Thai and Indonesian. Save it now: on a holiday, when many shops are shut, it is the quickest way to find out what is open.
